title: US Citizenship: 100 Civics Questions (2008 version)

sources.name: USCIS original 2008 question list, U.S. Government Publishing Office archive
U.S. House historical party government table, checked 2026-10-09

description: For learners using the 2008 USCIS civics test: 100 official questions and accepted answers. State-specific answers need personalization; officeholders need rechecking. Confirm your required test version and verify with current guidelines.

cards.front: What is the supreme law of the land?
cards.back: The Constitution.

cards.front: What does the Constitution do?
cards.back: Any one: sets up the government; defines the government; protects basic rights of Americans.

cards.front: The idea of self-government is in the first three words of the Constitution. What are these words?
cards.back: We the People.

cards.front: What is an amendment?
cards.back: A change to the Constitution; or an addition to the Constitution.

cards.front: What do we call the first ten amendments to the Constitution?
cards.back: The Bill of Rights.

cards.front: What is one right or freedom from the First Amendment?
cards.back: Any one: speech; religion; assembly; press; petition the government.

cards.front: How many amendments does the Constitution have?
cards.back: Twenty-seven (27).

cards.front: What did the Declaration of Independence do?
cards.back: Any one: announced our independence from Great Britain; declared our independence from Great Britain; said that the United States is free from Great Britain.

cards.front: What are two rights in the Declaration of Independence?
cards.back: Any two: life; liberty; pursuit of happiness.

cards.front: What is freedom of religion?
cards.back: You can practice any religion, or not practice a religion.

cards.front: What is the economic system in the United States?
cards.back: Capitalist economy; or market economy.

cards.front: What is the “rule of law”?
cards.back: Any one: everyone must follow the law; leaders must obey the law; government must obey the law; no one is above the law.

cards.front: Name one branch or part of the government.
cards.back: Any one: Congress (legislative); President (executive); the courts (judicial).

cards.front: What stops one branch of government from becoming too powerful?
cards.back: Checks and balances; or separation of powers.

cards.front: Who is in charge of the executive branch?
cards.back: The President.

cards.front: Who makes federal laws?
cards.back: Congress; the Senate and House of Representatives; or the U.S. (national) legislature.

cards.front: What are the two parts of the U.S. Congress?
cards.back: The Senate and House of Representatives.

cards.front: How many U.S. Senators are there?
cards.back: One hundred (100).

cards.front: We elect a U.S. Senator for how many years?
cards.back: Six (6).

cards.front: Who is one of your state’s U.S. Senators now?
cards.back: Answers vary by state and interview date: name either current U.S. Senator for your state. District of Columbia and U.S. territory residents should say that D.C. or their territory has no U.S. Senators. Find your state at senate.gov/senators.
cards.hint: Personalize this answer for where you live; current officeholders must match your interview date.

cards.front: The House of Representatives has how many voting members?
cards.back: Four hundred thirty-five (435).

cards.front: We elect a U.S. Representative for how many years?
cards.back: Two (2).

cards.front: Name your U.S. Representative.
cards.back: Answers vary by congressional district and interview date: give the current representative for your home address. Residents of territories with nonvoting Delegates or Resident Commissioners may name that official or say they have no voting Representative. Find your district at house.gov/representatives/find-your-representative.
cards.hint: Personalize this answer for where you live; current officeholders must match your interview date.

cards.front: Who does a U.S. Senator represent?
cards.back: All people of the state.

cards.front: Why do some states have more Representatives than other states?
cards.back: Because of the state's population; because they have more people; or because some states have more people.

cards.front: We elect a President for how many years?
cards.back: Four (4).

cards.front: In what month do we vote for President?
cards.back: November.

cards.front: What is the name of the President of the United States now?
cards.back: Donald Trump (Donald J. Trump). Verified against the White House reference on 2026-10-09. Give the official serving at your interview; recheck uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates.
cards.hint: This answer can change. Check the official USCIS test updates before your interview.

cards.front: What is the name of the Vice President of the United States now?
cards.back: JD Vance. Verified against the White House reference on 2026-10-09. Give the official serving at your interview; recheck uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates.
cards.hint: This answer can change. Check the official USCIS test updates before your interview.

cards.front: If the President can no longer serve, who becomes President?
cards.back: The Vice President.

cards.front: If both the President and the Vice President can no longer serve, who becomes President?
cards.back: The Speaker of the House.

cards.front: Who is the Commander in Chief of the military?
cards.back: The President.

cards.front: Who signs bills to become laws?
cards.back: The President.

cards.front: Who vetoes bills?
cards.back: The President.

cards.front: What does the President’s Cabinet do?
cards.back: Advises the President.

cards.front: What are two Cabinet-level positions?
cards.back: Any two, for example: Secretary of State and Attorney General. Other accepted positions in the 2008 list include Secretary of Agriculture, Commerce, Defense, Education, Energy, Health and Human Services, Homeland Security, Housing and Urban Development, the Interior, Labor, Transportation, the Treasury, and Veterans Affairs; and Vice President.

cards.front: What does the judicial branch do?
cards.back: Any one: reviews laws; explains laws; resolves disputes (disagreements); decides if a law goes against the Constitution.

cards.front: What is the highest court in the United States?
cards.back: The Supreme Court.

cards.front: How many justices are on the Supreme Court?
cards.back: Nine (9). Verified against the Supreme Court reference on 2026-10-09. Membership can change; recheck uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates before your interview.
cards.hint: This answer can change. Check the official USCIS test updates before your interview.

cards.front: Who is the Chief Justice of the United States now?
cards.back: John Roberts (John G. Roberts, Jr.). Verified against the Supreme Court reference on 2026-10-09. Give the official serving at your interview; recheck uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates.
cards.hint: This answer can change. Check the official USCIS test updates before your interview.

cards.front: Under our Constitution, some powers belong to the federal government. What is one power of the federal government?
cards.back: Any one: to print money; to declare war; to create an army; to make treaties.

cards.front: Under our Constitution, some powers belong to the states. What is one power of the states?
cards.back: Any one: provide schooling and education; provide protection (police); provide safety (fire departments); give a driver's license; approve zoning and land use.

cards.front: Who is the Governor of your state now?
cards.back: Answers vary by state and interview date: name your current governor. District of Columbia residents should say, “We don't have a Governor.” Verify using your official state government website before the interview.
cards.hint: Personalize this answer for where you live; current officeholders must match your interview date.

cards.front: What is the capital of your state?
cards.back: Answers vary: name your state's capital. District of Columbia residents should say that D.C. is not a state and does not have a capital. Residents of U.S. territories should name their territory's capital.
cards.hint: Personalize this answer for where you live; current officeholders must match your interview date.

cards.front: What are the two major political parties in the United States?
cards.back: Democratic and Republican.

cards.front: What is the political party of the President now?
cards.back: Republican Party, for President Donald Trump. Verified against the U.S. House party-government table on 2026-10-09. Give the party of the official serving at your interview; recheck uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates.
cards.hint: This answer can change. Check the official USCIS test updates before your interview.

cards.front: What is the name of the Speaker of the House of Representatives now?
cards.back: Mike Johnson. Verified against the Speaker's official website on 2026-10-09. Give the official serving at your interview; recheck uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates.
cards.hint: This answer can change. Check the official USCIS test updates before your interview.

cards.front: There are four amendments to the Constitution about who can vote. Describe one of them.
cards.back: Any one: citizens eighteen (18) and older can vote; you don't have to pay a poll tax to vote; any citizen can vote (women and men can vote); a male citizen of any race can vote.

cards.front: What is one responsibility that is only for United States citizens?
cards.back: Serve on a jury; or vote in a federal election.

cards.front: Name one right only for United States citizens.
cards.back: Vote in a federal election; or run for federal office.

cards.front: What are two rights of everyone living in the United States?
cards.back: Any two: freedom of expression; freedom of speech; freedom of assembly; freedom to petition the government; freedom of worship; the right to bear arms.

cards.front: What do we show loyalty to when we say the Pledge of Allegiance?
cards.back: The United States; or the flag.

cards.front: What is one promise you make when you become a United States citizen?
cards.back: Any one: give up loyalty to other countries; defend the Constitution and laws of the United States; obey the laws of the United States; serve in the U.S. military if needed; serve (do important work for) the nation if needed; be loyal to the United States.

cards.front: How old do citizens have to be to vote for President?
cards.back: Eighteen (18) and older.

cards.front: What are two ways that Americans can participate in their democracy?
cards.back: Any two: vote; join a political party; help with a campaign; join a civic group; join a community group; give an elected official your opinion on an issue; call Senators and Representatives; publicly support or oppose an issue or policy; run for office; write to a newspaper.

cards.front: When is the last day you can send in federal income tax forms?
cards.back: April 15 is the listed 2008 civics-test answer. Actual filing deadlines can differ by year or circumstances; this card is the test answer, not tax-filing advice.

cards.front: When must all men register for the Selective Service?
cards.back: At age eighteen (18); or between eighteen (18) and twenty-six (26), as worded in the official civics list. This is the test answer; current eligibility and registration rules require separate verification.

cards.front: What is one reason colonists came to America?
cards.back: Any one: freedom; political liberty; religious freedom; economic opportunity; practice their religion; escape persecution.

cards.front: Who lived in America before the Europeans arrived?
cards.back: American Indians; or Native Americans.

cards.front: What group of people was taken to America and sold as slaves?
cards.back: Africans; or people from Africa.

cards.front: Why did the colonists fight the British?
cards.back: Any one: because of high taxes (taxation without representation); because the British army stayed in their houses (boarding, quartering); because they didn't have self-government.

cards.front: Who wrote the Declaration of Independence?
cards.back: Thomas Jefferson.

cards.front: When was the Declaration of Independence adopted?
There were 13 original states. Name three.
cards.back: Any three: New Hampshire; Massachusetts; Rhode Island; Connecticut; New York; New Jersey; Pennsylvania; Delaware; Maryland; Virginia; North Carolina; South Carolina; Georgia.

cards.front: What happened at the Constitutional Convention?
cards.back: The Constitution was written; or the Founding Fathers wrote the Constitution.

cards.front: When was the Constitution written?
The Federalist Papers supported the passage of the U.S. Constitution. Name one of the writers.
cards.back: Any one: James Madison; Alexander Hamilton; John Jay; Publius.

cards.front: What is one thing Benjamin Franklin is famous for?
cards.back: Any one: U.S. diplomat; oldest member of the Constitutional Convention; first Postmaster General of the United States; writer of Poor Richard's Almanac; started the first free libraries.

cards.front: Who is the “Father of Our Country”?
cards.back: George Washington.

cards.front: Who was the first President?
cards.back: George Washington.

cards.front: What territory did the United States buy from France in 1803?
cards.back: The Louisiana Territory; or Louisiana.

cards.front: Name one war fought by the United States in the 1800s.
cards.back: Any one: War of 1812; Mexican-American War; Civil War; Spanish-American War.

cards.front: Name the U.S. war between the North and the South.
cards.back: The Civil War; or the War between the States.

cards.front: Name one problem that led to the Civil War.
cards.back: Any one listed test answer: slavery; economic reasons; states' rights.

cards.front: What was one important thing that Abraham Lincoln did?
cards.back: Any one: freed the slaves (Emancipation Proclamation); saved (or preserved) the Union; led the United States during the Civil War.

cards.front: What did the Emancipation Proclamation do?
cards.back: An accepted answer is “freed slaves in the Confederacy.” The list also accepts “freed the slaves,” “freed slaves in the Confederate states,” or “freed slaves in most Southern states.” Historically, it applied to designated areas in rebellion, not every enslaved person nationwide.

cards.front: What did Susan B. Anthony do?
cards.back: Fought for women's rights; or fought for civil rights.

cards.front: Name one war fought by the United States in the 1900s.
cards.back: Any one: World War I; World War II; Korean War; Vietnam War; Persian Gulf War.

cards.front: Who was President during World War I?
cards.back: Woodrow Wilson.

cards.front: Who was President during the Great Depression and World War II?
cards.back: Franklin Roosevelt (Franklin D. Roosevelt).

cards.front: Who did the United States fight in World War II?
cards.back: Japan, Germany, and Italy.

cards.front: Before he was President, Eisenhower was a general. What war was he in?
cards.back: World War II.

cards.front: During the Cold War, what was the main concern of the United States?
cards.back: Communism.

cards.front: What movement tried to end racial discrimination?
cards.back: The civil rights movement.

cards.front: What did Martin Luther King, Jr. do?
cards.back: Fought for civil rights; or worked for equality for all Americans.

cards.front: What major event happened on September 11, 2001, in the United States?
cards.back: Terrorists attacked the United States.

cards.front: Name one American Indian tribe in the United States.
cards.back: Any one listed example: Cherokee; Navajo; Sioux; Chippewa; Choctaw; Pueblo; Apache; Iroquois; Creek; Blackfeet; Seminole; Cheyenne; Arawak; Shawnee; Mohegan; Huron; Oneida; Lakota; Crow; Teton; Hopi; Inuit. These reproduce the official list's terminology.

cards.front: Name one of the two longest rivers in the United States.
cards.back: Missouri River; or Mississippi River.

cards.front: What ocean is on the West Coast of the United States?
cards.back: Pacific Ocean.

cards.front: What ocean is on the East Coast of the United States?
cards.back: Atlantic Ocean.

cards.front: Name one U.S. territory.
cards.back: Any one: Puerto Rico; U.S. Virgin Islands; American Samoa; Northern Mariana Islands; Guam.

cards.front: Name one state that borders Canada.
cards.back: Any one: Maine; New Hampshire; Vermont; New York; Pennsylvania; Ohio; Michigan; Minnesota; North Dakota; Montana; Idaho; Washington; Alaska.

cards.front: Name one state that borders Mexico.
cards.back: Any one: California; Arizona; New Mexico; Texas.

cards.front: What is the capital of the United States?
cards.back: Washington, D.C.

cards.front: Where is the Statue of Liberty?
cards.back: New York Harbor; or Liberty Island. The official list also accepts New Jersey, near New York City, and on the Hudson River.

cards.front: Why does the flag have 13 stripes?
cards.back: Because there were 13 original colonies; or because the stripes represent the original colonies.

cards.front: Why does the flag have 50 stars?
cards.back: Because there is one star for each state; because each star represents a state; or because there are 50 states.

cards.front: What is the name of the national anthem?
cards.back: The Star-Spangled Banner.

cards.front: When do we celebrate Independence Day?
cards.back: July 4.

cards.front: Name two national U.S. holidays.
cards.back: Any two from the 2008 list: New Year's Day; Martin Luther King, Jr., Day; Presidents' Day; Memorial Day; Independence Day; Labor Day; Columbus Day; Veterans Day; Thanksgiving; Christmas.
